beur-hagra/1:א: (א) Forbidden to say regarding any animal — even if it is not a kid or lamb. Rosh, according to Rashi, that the reason is that they will say one consecrated it for the monetary value of the Paschal offering, whether large or small. Beit Yosef from the reason stated above, and so too from the Gemara there that he only brought out wheat and did not distinguish between one animal and another animal.
beur-hagra/1:ב: (ב) Whether — as stated above, "this meat," whether slaughtered.
beur-hagra/1:ג: (ג) That it appears one consecrated it, etc. This is according to Tosafos, and specifically a kid and lamb; but according to Rashi, because it appears one consecrated it for the monetary value of the Paschal offering as stated above, and so too in Yerushalmi chapter 7 of Pesachim 5:1, that it is forbidden for a person to say to his fellow: "Here is the money, go and buy me meat for Passover"; but he says to him: "Here is this money, go and buy me meat for roasting."
beur-hagra/1:ה: (ה) And a kid, etc., but, etc. — Gemara there.
chok-yaakov/1:א: (א) Forbidden to say regarding any animal. And Maharil forbids even fowl, anything of its species that requires shechita; and it is an extra stringency that he was so stringent (Bach and Magen Avraham). And see in the Rokeach siman 474 that he also wrote as the opinion of Maharil, see there; and below siman 476. And the author's brother-in-law in his book Or Zarua wrote that even in fish and the like it is forbidden, because it is possible one consecrated them for their value since one said "for Passover," which is not so regarding wheat that require guarding — we say one means "I am guarding it for Passover." And his words are correct to be careful l'chatchila; and b'dieved, if one said "this meat for Passover," as the Bach wrote, it is forbidden even for benefit (and in truth his words contradict what he wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 5, and I expanded on this in my commentary to Tur Yoreh De'ah; and now that Peri Chadash was printed I saw he also sensed this difficulty, see there). And Eliyah Rabbah and Taz permit even in eating, and so too Magen Avraham in the name of Shach — but he concluded "this requires further study," for the Bach brings proof from the Gemara to which there is no answer; therefore it appears to me that in a kid and lamb one should be stringent b'dieved, and in other meat one should not be stringent — end of his words Magen Avraham. And in my humble opinion, as the agreement of other later authorities, one does not forbid at all b'dieved. And what the Bach brought as proof from a passage in Shas that it is forbidden even b'dieved — if because of this it does not apply, for Shas concludes there on daf 33 according to R' Shimon, who holds that anyone who did not vow in the manner of those who vow — his words are nothing — there is no prohibition if one said "this meat for Passover" (and see in Tosafos s.v. mipnei she'nireh). And if so, since we rule thus, the halacha is as R' Shimon, as Rambam ruled chapter 16 of Laws of Sacrificial Procedure; therefore one does not forbid at all b'dieved, only a general stringency — l'chatchila they are stringent. And the later authorities well attained against the Bach in this; examine carefully.
chok-yaakov/1:ב: (ב) "This meat for Passover." And Magen Avraham wrote: what people are accustomed to say in a foreign language "this meat for Passover" — there is no concern; for if it were that one consecrated it, one should have said "this meat for Passover" — end of his words. And so is the custom to say thus, and people are not particular.
chok-yaakov/1:ג: (ג) "This for Passover." And the Rokeach wrote siman 283: one should not say "how much trouble is Passover." In the Yerushalmi: the wicked one — what does he say? "What is this work for you?" "And how much trouble is this" — end of his words. And all the decisors did not mention this warning; also I did not see people careful about it. And it appears to me that they explain the Yerushalmi specifically regarding the Paschal offering — it is forbidden to say "what is this work for you," for it appears there is a d'oraisa commandment upon him to trouble himself. Which is not so in this time, where one only speaks of the greatness of caution and extra stringencies — "how much trouble" — there is no concern; so it appears to me.
peri-megadim/1:_: Forbidden — Magen Avraham permitted b'dieved, not as Bach; and so agreed Eliyah Rabbah; and Magen Avraham 2 brings proof from Pesachim 53b, that a kid mekulas is forbidden in eating to eat thus; but if one roasted it thus mekulas and afterward cut it into limbs — if so, that also in mekulas it is permitted and it is not forbidden because one roasted it all as one; and the same is true when one says "this meat for Passover" — it is not forbidden b'dieved by declaration for eating. And what is stated at the beginning of siman 476, and in many places, that it is forbidden to eat what is roasted all as one — even in a place where one eats roasted meat, it is forbidden to place it on the table whole because of viewers; rather one cuts into limbs before placing on the table. And in Rambam's Laws of the Paschal Offering chapter 10 it implies eating the Paschal offering while it is still whole on the table, and one cuts the meat from above and afterward, if he wishes, cuts the bones between the joints; and see Olas Shabbat, who explicitly permitted a kid mekulas if one roasted it as one to cut into limbs and it is permitted to eat. And that which is stated in Pesachim 4:1: what is a kid mekulas that is forbidden to eat in this time — that is, to eat whole; but if one cuts into limbs, it is permitted — somewhat strained. And the language of Taz in 476 may be explained simply: if one roasted as one, it is forbidden to eat afterward when one cuts into limbs before placing on the table. And what Taz wrote: although in mekulas it is forbidden in eating — there, because of eating it will appear as though one consecrated it, that is, if one eats at the time of eating whole — it is obvious that this is its prohibition; but if one roasted as one and cut it into limbs, even mekulas is permitted in eating in a place where they eat roasted meat. And what is stated: and in a kid mekulas too there is prohibition in making it — apparently he brought proof and evidence that mekulas in making is forbidden, as the language of Tur and Rambam; and if so, in 476 why did they write forbidden to eat roasted as one — also cutting it is forbidden? We learn: because of making there is no prohibition; likewise declaration — there is no prohibition in eating. And one may say: below, forbidden to eat roasted as one — even if one cuts afterward before placing on the table into limbs — except his apparent intention is that mekulas, eating too is forbidden; how did Rambam write "a kid mekulas is forbidden to make it" — it implies it is comparable to saying "this meat for Passover"; but it is not so according to this explanation, that in mekulas there is also prohibition in making — strained. And one may say simply: a kid mekulas has two prohibitions: (1) to make it whole with its head and innards — forbidden in making; (2) forbidden to eat whole — and proof from Beitzah 22b: "and they make a kid mekulas, and the Sages forbid" — it implies making too is forbidden (and according to Beit Yosef it implies from Pesachim 52, and "this requires further study"). And accordingly, it is difficult what Rambam wrote, as below 476 — there he speaks of eating; and according to this explanation — no. Eating is forbidden from the time of making, and "this requires further study." And it implies from Taz: even a live sheep fit for Passover, and one said "this for Passover" — anything one did not explicitly consecrate is permitted b'dieved, and "this requires further study"; and see Yoreh De'ah siman 5 on this.
